finding.claim: deleteAccount calls canDelete() but discards the boolean result, so the authorization check is never enforced. Any caller can delete any account. closeAccount correctly uses assertCanDelete, which shows the intended pattern.
finding.source: Any authenticated user calling DELETE /accounts/{id} with an arbitrary account id

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) is the entry point for DELETE /accounts/{id}; id is attacker-controlled
Account is looked up by the caller-supplied id with no ownership filter
canDelete(u, a) returns a boolean that is ignored, so there is no throw or return
accounts.remove(id) runs unconditionally, deleting another user's account (IDOR / broken access control)

finding.guards_checked: The check at line 22 does not guard anything because its result is unused. No other authorization appears in the file, and there is no caller or framework layer in the repo. The sibling closeAccount at line 29 uses assertCanDelete, which throws. A non-existent id gives a null Account, so canDelete would NPE if its result were used, but the missing-check path still removes the entry.

verdict.guard_found: canDelete (line 9) returns a boolean but is a bare statement at line 22, so its result is discarded. assertCanDelete (line 13) would throw but is only used in closeAccount. No other guard exists.
verdict.reason: src/AccountService.java:22 calls the boolean canDelete() and ignores its result, so accounts.remove(id) at line 23 runs for any authenticated user and any id, unlike closeAccount, which uses the throwing assertCanDelete at line 29.
